a: My conscience bears witness along with me in the Holy Spirit
t: Paul swears an oath, and calls his conscience as a witness
p: Paul piles up three guarantees that he is not exaggerating his grief.
b: Paul opens with something close to an oath: "in Christ" (as one who belongs to Christ), "I am not lying" and his conscience as a co-witness "in the Holy Spirit." The Greek word for conscience is syneidesis, literally "knowing together with oneself" (also 2:15 and 13:5). Why the oath? He is about to say that he would give up his place in Christ for his people (9:3), and he knows his Gentile readers in Rome may have heard that he is an enemy of Israel and its law (compare Acts 21:21). The next three chapters are not a lecture on predestination that happens to mention Israel. They begin with a Jew's broken heart.

a: I would even wish to be cursed myself, cut off from Christ
t: "I would wish": a wish Paul knows he cannot have
p: The Greek verb is in a tense that can mean "I was wishing" or "I would wish." Paul echoes Moses.
b: Euchomen is the imperfect of a verb for wishing or praying, with no "would" word. Readings: "I was wishing" (a wish he once had), "I could wish" (if it were possible), or "I would wish" (the imperfect of a wish that cannot come true, as in Philemon 13, "I would have liked to keep him" in the Greek). Most commentators take it as an unreal wish that Paul knows cannot be granted, since 8:35-39 says nothing can cut a believer off from Christ's love. Anathema means something handed over to God for destruction (the Septuagint uses it for the "ban" of Joshua 6:17-18). The closest model is Moses, who asked God to wipe him from his book if God would not forgive the golden calf: "And now, if you will forgive their sin... But if not, wipe me out, please, from your book that you have written" (Exodus 32:32).
orig: ηὐχόμην ... ἀνάθεμα (euchomen ... anathema), 'I was wishing ... a curse'

a: my relatives according to the flesh
t: "Brothers" here means family by blood
p: Paul uses the Church's word for believers, "brothers," for Jews who do not believe.
b: In most of the letter "brothers" means fellow believers. The Greek plural adelphoi is also used of mixed groups of men and women (Acts 1:15; 21:17; 28:14), so it can be read "brothers and sisters"; the Plain keeps the form used in Acts (see Romans 1:13). Here the word is stretched: Paul calls unbelieving Jews his adelphoi, his syngeneis (relatives), "according to the flesh," meaning by physical descent. "Flesh" in this verse is not sinful nature. It is the ordinary word for blood ties and shared descent, as in 9:5 and 9:8. The phrase tells Gentile readers that Paul does not stop being Israel's kin when he becomes an apostle to the Gentiles.

a: They are Israelites
t: Israel's list of gifts: why Paul begins with them
p: Before he argues, Paul lists what God gave to Israel, and starts with "who are Israelites," in the present tense.
b: "Israelite" is the covenant name, from the name God gave Jacob (Genesis 32:28), and Paul uses it of himself (11:1; 2 Corinthians 11:22). Paul lists six gifts here and adds two more in 9:5 (the patriarchs and the Messiah). Paul writes "who are Israelites" in the present tense. The gifts that follow have no verb of their own in the Greek, and the Plain supplies "is." Commentators divide on whether Paul means the gifts as present possessions or as past ones, so the tense is not proof either way. Whether the gifts still belong to Israel as a nation, or only to believing Israel, is the question that drives chapters 9-11, and Christians have answered it differently (see the cards at 9:6 and 11:26). Krister Stendahl and many Jewish readers point to this list as Paul's own evidence that he did not teach that God had finished with the Jews.

a: the adoption as children
t: Adoption: God's firstborn son was a nation
p: Israel was called God's son before the church was called God's adopted children.
b: Huiothesia, literally "placing as a son," was a Greek legal word for adoption. God told Pharaoh, "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22), and Hosea 11:1 says God loved Israel when he was a boy. Paul will use the same word for believers (8:15, 23). So the church's adoption (Romans 8:15) is not a replacement of Israel's but a sharing in it, a point Jewish readers and the New Perspective both stress.

a: the covenants
t: Why "covenants," plural
p: Paul counts more than one covenant: with Abraham, at Sinai and with David.
b: The plural fits the Old Testament story: God's covenants with Noah, with Abraham (Genesis 15; 17), with Israel at Sinai (Exodus 24), with Phinehas (Numbers 25:13) and with David (2 Samuel 7), and the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31-34, which Paul may echo in 11:27. The list matters because 11:29 argues that God's gifts are not taken back, and covenants are God's own oaths.
r: Genesis 15; Genesis 17; Exodus 24; Numbers 25:13; 2 Samuel 7; Jeremiah 31:31; Romans 11:27

a: the sacred service
t: The worship in the sanctuary
p: "Service" is Paul's word for the whole system of sacrifices and priests.
b: Latreia is service rendered to God, and in the Greek Bible it nearly always means the Temple worship with its offerings (for example Exodus 12:25-26, where the Septuagint uses it of the Passover service). Paul uses the same word of believers in 12:1, where "your living sacrifice" is called your latreia. The Plain says "sacred service" so a reader can see both uses. The Temple still stood when Paul wrote, so for him this was a present gift, not a memory.

a: in his human descent
t: The Messiah is a Jew
p: Paul's own gospel says Jesus came from Israel, in his human line.
b: To kata sarka means "as far as the flesh is concerned," that is, his physical descent. The little phrase also hints at a contrast Paul made in 1:3-4: "from David's seed according to the flesh" and "Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness." The phrase says Jesus is a descendant of Abraham and David. It also holds back something: if Christ also has another side beyond the flesh, then "according to the flesh" is exactly what you would write if the next words were "who is over everything, God blessed forever" (see the note on that phrase). In Paul's day this was a pointed thing to say to Gentile Christians in Rome: your Lord is a Jew.
orig: τὸ κατὰ σάρκα (to kata sarka), 'as to the flesh'

a: who is over everything, God blessed forever
t: Does Paul call Christ "God" here?
p: The Greek has no punctuation. Where you put a period decides whether Paul calls Christ God.
b: The oldest manuscripts have no commas or periods, so every edition must choose. Three readings: (1) About Christ: "the Christ, who is over everything, God blessed forever," which calls Christ God. (2) A doxology to the Father: "the Christ according to the flesh. God, who is over all, be blessed forever." (3) Christ over all, then praise: "the Christ, who is over all. God be blessed forever." Reading (1) was held by Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.16.3), Tertullian (Against Praxeas 13) and Chrysostom, and now by Metzger, Cranfield, Murray, Moo, Fitzmyer, Dunn and N. T. Wright. Käsemann is often cited for (2). For (1): "who is" normally describes the noun before it, and in Jewish blessings "blessed" comes before the name of God (2 Corinthians 1:3). For (2): Paul seldom calls Christ theos (Titus 2:13 is the nearest, in a letter whose authorship is debated; John 20:28 is John, not Paul), and praise fits the list of Israel's privileges. See the variant entry for the editions.

a: God's word has failed
t: The question behind chapters 9-11
p: If Israel does not believe, did God's promises fall to the ground?
b: Ekpipto is "fall off" or "fall to the ground," the word used of a flower dropping its petals (1 Peter 1:24, quoting Isaiah) or a ship running aground (Acts 27:17). Paul's thesis for 9-11 is that God's "word" (his promise to Israel) has not dropped. He will hold to that, through the remnant (9:27; 11:5) and the final salvation (11:26), and he ends in praise of a God whose gifts are not taken back (11:29). Notice that the thing under attack is God's faithfulness, not Israel's. That is why the chapters keep returning to the words "mercy" and "calling."

a: not everyone who is from Israel is Israel
t: Two Israels? Paul's most disputed sentence
p: Paul says that being born into Israel is not the same as being Israel in God's eyes. What he means is disputed.
b: The line is the hinge for the church-and-Israel debate. Readings: (1) Israel within Israel: a faithful core inside the nation, the chosen remnant (9:27; 11:5), held by many commentators (Moo, Cranfield); N. T. Wright, who reads Israel as redefined around the Messiah, stands between this reading and the next. (2) The church is the true or new Israel, a reading found among the fathers (Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 123-125) and in much Protestant covenant theology, which argues from Galatians 6:16, Philippians 3:3 and Ephesians 2:11-22 that the titles of Israel now belong to all who are in Christ and denies that this rejects the Jews. Against this, Paul never calls the church "Israel" in Romans, and in 11:25-26 "Israel" must mean the Jewish people (compare Galatians 6:16, the one place where "the Israel of God" is debated). (3) A call to Israel's own history: Isaac and Jacob show that God has always chosen inside Abraham's family, and the point is that God's choice is free, not that anyone is cast out (Jewish and Messianic Jewish readers). (4) No new Israel at all: Israel stays Israel; Gentiles are joined to it (11:17; Ephesians 2:12-13). Words in 9:6 and 11:26 are the same word "Israel." Whether it means the same thing in both is the question.

a: Your offspring will be named through Isaac
t: Genesis 21:12: Isaac, not Ishmael
p: Paul quotes the Greek Genesis, where God tells Abraham which son carries the promise.
b: The quotation is Genesis 21:12 in the Septuagint. This site's Plain of the Hebrew reads: "for it is through Isaac that offspring will be named for you" (Genesis 21:12). "Named" (kaleo, "call") means counted, recognized as your line. Ishmael was also Abraham's son by flesh, and so were Keturah's sons (Genesis 25:1-4); Esau, as Isaac's son, is Abraham's grandson and also his offspring. Paul's argument: Abraham's physical descent never was the test. He uses Sarah's son again in Galatians 4:21-31 for a different point.

a: born by the flesh
t: "Flesh" and "promise": two ways of being born
p: Isaac's birth was by God's promise at a time when his parents were past hope.
b: "Flesh" in this verse is again ordinary human descent. The contrast Paul draws is not between Jews and Gentiles. It is between births that happen by nature and a birth that happens because God said it would (Genesis 18:10, 14). Sarah was far past childbearing years; Paul makes the same point of Abraham's faith in 4:19. The "children of the promise" are those whose existence rests on God's word, and Paul will include Gentiles among them (9:24-26).

a: At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son
t: Genesis 18:10, 14
p: A promise made to a woman who laughed.
b: Paul blends the Septuagint of Genesis 18:10 and 18:14. This site's Plain of Genesis 18:10 reads "I will surely come back to you when the season comes round again, and Sarah your wife will have a son" (Genesis 18:10). The point of the quotation is its form: God says "I will come," and a son is born, with no human act in between. That is the pattern of "promise" that Paul wants his readers to see.

a: based on his choosing
t: "Based on his choosing": individuals or nations?
p: The first big step in Paul's argument: God's purpose runs by choice, not by merit.
b: Paul calls God's plan a purpose (prothesis) that works "by election" (kat' eklogen). Two readings are common. (1) Individual election to salvation: God chose Jacob and passed over Esau as persons before birth, and the same holds for every believer (Augustine, Calvin, the Canons of Dort, Piper). (2) Corporate or historical election: Jacob and Esau stand for the peoples Israel and Edom (Genesis 25:23; Malachi 1:2-3), and God's choice is of a people for a role in history, not of each person's eternal fate (Abasciano; Wright and Dunn put it in terms of God's choice of Israel for the world's sake; Wesley read Romans 9 of peoples and roles). (3) Conditional individual election: God elects persons, but in Christ and in response to faith (Arminius). A further group says the chapter is about both persons and peoples. Catholic and Orthodox views are set out in the card. The traditions card on this chapter gives each church's own wording.

a: not by works but by the one who calls
t: The verse split
p: In the Greek text this clause belongs to the start of 9:12; in the KJV numbering it ends 9:11.
b: The SBL Greek text puts "not from works but from the one who calls" at the start of its verse 12, while the KJV and most English Bibles end verse 11 with it. This site keeps the KJV numbering, so the clause stays here and 9:12 starts with the words "She was told." The sense is the same either way. The "one who calls" (ho kalōn) is God, and the call is what makes someone one of the called (8:28, 30; 9:24).

a: The elder will serve the younger
t: Genesis 25:23: two nations in one womb
p: God's word to Rebecca was about two peoples, though Paul uses it for two persons.
b: In Genesis the LORD tells Rebecca: "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will divide from your body. One people will be stronger than the other, and the elder will serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23). Esau became Edom and Jacob became Israel. The oracle speaks of nations, and Edom did serve Israel under David (2 Samuel 8:14), so Paul's quotation gives support to the reading that the argument concerns peoples. Those who hold individual election note that Paul asks the question of persons ("Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated"). Notice also that the older serving the younger overturns the custom of the firstborn's right, a repeated pattern in Genesis (Isaac over Ishmael, Joseph over his brothers, Judah over Reuben).

a: I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau
t: "Hated": the Hebrew idiom of preferring
p: In Hebrew and Greek speech, "love" and "hate" can mean choosing one over the other.
b: Paul quotes Malachi 1:2-3, where God speaks about the nations, not the twin brothers: Edom, Esau's descendants, lay in ruins. The verb "hate" in such pairs does not mean a feeling of loathing. The Old Testament says Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and calls Leah "the unloved one" (Genesis 29:30-31), and the law about a man with two wives uses "loved" and "unloved" for first and second place (Deuteronomy 21:15-16). In the same way, Jesus says a disciple must "hate" his family, meaning put them second (Luke 14:26). Many Reformed commentators accept the idiom and still hold that Esau's line is passed over; others (Wesley) read the verse of the peoples and not of each person. Translators who write "hated" are being literal. Readers should not assume the English word's full strength.

a: Is God unjust? By no means!
t: The diatribe style: question, "By no means!"
p: Paul pretends to hear an objector and answers him in the manner of a classroom debate.
b: "By no means" (me genoito, literally "may it not be") is the hallmark of the ancient teacher's debate with an imagined opponent, called the diatribe (Stowers). Paul used it in 3:4, 6, 31; 6:2, 15; 7:7, 13. It rejects the question without arguing the point; the arguing comes in the verses after. The accusation, "Is God adikos?", means unjust or unfair. It is the opposite of dikaios, from the same root as "righteousness," a link the English "unjust" hides (3:5 asks the same question). Paul's answer in 9:15 is surprising: he does not argue that the outcome is fair by human standards; he appeals to God's own mercy.
orig: μὴ γένοιτο (me genoito), 'may it not be!'; ἀδικία (adikia), 'injustice'

a: I will show mercy to whoever I show mercy
t: Exodus 33:19: God's answer after the golden calf
p: In the original story God says this to Moses just after Israel worshiped a calf.
b: Paul quotes Exodus 33:19 in the Septuagint, which has "I will show mercy... and have compassion," where the Hebrew has "I will be gracious... and show pity." This site's Plain of the Hebrew reads: "I will show grace to whoever I show grace, and pity whoever I pity" (Exodus 33:19). The context in Exodus is not about Pharaoh or the lost. It follows Israel's sin with the golden calf, when God could have ended the people, and Moses begged. God answered with a statement of his freedom to forgive: he is free to show mercy to those who do not deserve it. Read that way, Paul's first example is of mercy shown to rebel Israel, not of rejection. Exodus 34:6-7, where God names himself "compassionate and gracious," follows directly.

a: not up to the one who wills, or the one who runs
t: Willing and running: is the human will cancelled?
p: The verse says mercy does not depend on human wanting or effort. What follows for free will?
b: "Wills" and "runs" name desire and effort (an athlete's word; compare 1 Corinthians 9:24). Augustine, Luther (The Bondage of the Will) and Calvin read the verse as saying that the will, on its own, can produce nothing toward salvation. Origen and Jerome, and later the Catholic Church and the Orthodox, read it as saying that human effort is not sufficient by itself: it must be joined by God's grace, which comes first (the Council of Trent's decree on justification, chapter 5; synergeia in Orthodox teaching). The traditions card at 9:16 sets these side by side.

a: I raised you up
t: Pharaoh: "raised up" in Greek, "caused to stand" in Hebrew
p: Paul changes the words of Exodus 9:16, and the three versions mean slightly different things.
b: The Hebrew of Exodus 9:16 says God "caused you to stand" (he'emadtikha), meaning kept you alive through the plagues. This site's Plain: "But for this reason I have kept you standing: to let you see my strength, and so that my name will be told in all the earth" (Exodus 9:16). The Septuagint has "you were kept" (dietērēthēs). Paul writes exegeira, "I raised up," which can mean "roused" or "brought on the stage" (like a king or a figure in history). Paul keeps the goal exactly: God's power shown and his name spread. The three wordings ask the reader to notice that Pharaoh was kept alive, not made evil.

a: he hardens whom he wants
t: Who hardened Pharaoh? The order in Exodus
p: Exodus says Pharaoh hardened his own heart and also that God did. The order matters for how churches read this verse.
b: Sklerynei is "makes hard." Exodus uses three Hebrew verbs (chazaq stubborn, kaved heavy, qashah hard). Readers have counted who is the subject. In the first plagues the text says Pharaoh's heart "was stubborn" (Exodus 7:13, 22; 8:19) or that Pharaoh "made his heart heavy" (Exodus 8:15, 32; 9:34). Only after the sixth plague: "But the LORD made Pharaoh's heart stubborn" (Exodus 9:12). But God announced it before any of it (Exodus 4:21; 7:3). Views: (1) God's hardening is the cause and Pharaoh's choices are the result (Calvin, Luther, Piper); (2) God hardens as a judgment on someone who already hardened himself (Origen, Wesley, many Arminian and Orthodox readers; Origen's picture: the same sun melts wax and hardens clay, On First Principles 3.1.10); (3) the verse is about Pharaoh's role in history, not his eternal salvation (many Catholic scholars). Paul does not say which. He makes the point of 9:17: God's freedom to use even a defiant king.

a: Then why does he still blame anyone?
t: The objector speaks: who is the "you"?
p: Paul's imagined opponent is a rhetorical figure, not a real person at Rome.
b: From 9:19 Paul speaks to an imagined opponent in the style of a diatribe (see the note on 9:14). He addresses him as "human being" (9:20), a plain word that sets human smallness against God. The objector is not a Jew in particular. The objection is the oldest one: if God decides, how can he judge? The Wisdom of Solomon (12:12) asks who could say to God, "What have you done?" (compare also Wisdom of Solomon 13-14 with Romans 1:18-32). The answer is not a proof. It is a reminder that creatures cannot sue their maker.
r: Romans 3:5-8; Wisdom of Solomon 12:12; Job 9:12; Job 40:2

a: who are you to argue against God
t: Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9: the clay answers back
p: Paul borrows the potter's picture from Isaiah, where it is a scolding to Israel.
b: The first source is Isaiah 29:16: "Is the potter to be counted the same as the clay, so that the thing made says of the one who made it, 'He did not make me'" (Isaiah 29:16). The second is Isaiah 45:9: "Woe to the one who argues with the one who formed him, a piece of pottery among the pieces of pottery on the ground" (Isaiah 45:9). In Isaiah both are spoken to Israel (the first to leaders who hide their plans from God, the second to people complaining that God is using Cyrus). So the clay in Isaiah is Israel talking back, not unbelievers. Paul fits the picture to his purposes. Notice the two verbs: "formed" (plasma) is the word of Genesis 2:7, and God forming Adam from dust is also in the background.

a: does the potter not have the authority
t: Jeremiah 18, Wisdom and Sirach: the potter is not only about power
p: The potter appears in several older texts. In Jeremiah, the clay can be remade if the people turn.
b: Most commentators think Jeremiah 18:1-12 stands behind this. There the LORD sends Jeremiah to a potter's house; a vessel is spoiled and the potter makes it over. God explains that if a nation he warned turns from evil he will relent, and if a nation turns from good he will change his plan. In the Wisdom of Solomon a potter who shapes idols from clay is mocked (15:7-13), and in Sirach people are "as clay in the potter's hand" (33:13). Reading it with Jeremiah makes the clay changeable, a point some use for the corporate reading: vessels of anger can still become vessels of mercy (11:23). Reading it with 9:22 as a strict decree makes the clay fixed. Paul does not mention Jeremiah by name.
r: Jeremiah 18:1-12; Isaiah 64:8; Wisdom of Solomon 15:7; Sirach 36:13; Romans 11:23

a: vessels of anger, fitted for destruction
t: "Fitted" (by whom?) and "prepared ahead of time"
p: A small grammatical choice in the Greek matters for who is responsible for destruction.
b: The two vessels are described with two different verbs. The vessels of mercy were "prepared ahead of time" by God (proetoimasen, active, 9:23). The vessels of anger were "fitted" (katertismena), a participle that is either passive (made ready by someone, by God or by themselves) or middle (made themselves ready). Chrysostom pointed out in his homilies on Romans that Paul says the vessels of mercy were prepared by God but does not say God fitted the others. Calvin, and Luther in The Bondage of the Will, take it as a passive with God as the agent. Many Orthodox and Arminian readers take it as reflexive, a judgment on those who made themselves ready. The grammar permits both; the difference between the two verbs is real.

a: What if God, wanting to show his anger
t: An unfinished sentence: "What if"
p: Paul asks "What if" and never finishes the sentence. The reader supplies the answer.
b: The Greek sentence of 9:22-24 has an "if" and no "then." Ancient Greek letters allow this rhetorical break (aposiopesis, a deliberate silence). The question is: could not God have the right, if he wished to show his anger and make his power known, to put up with those who deserved it, for a longer time, in order also to show the riches of his mercy? Notice "bore with much patience": even the vessels of anger receive patience. Some commentators (Wright, Dunn) see this as a description of what God did with Israel during the long years before the exile and the cross: patience first, judgment delayed. Matthew 23:37 and Luke 19:41-44 show Jesus lamenting over the city in similar terms (Luke 19:41 says he wept).

a: not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles
t: The called are Jews and Gentiles
p: The "vessels of mercy" include both groups. The thread of chapter 9 turns here toward the Gentiles.
b: Until this verse the discussion looked as if it were all about who inside Israel is chosen. Here Paul says that the called are not a subgroup of Israel only: they are "out of" the Jews and "out of" the Gentiles (compare 10:12). The word "called" (kaleo) now echoes 9:7, 12 and 25-26. It is a hinge. Readers who think of the church as the new Israel find here its first support; readers who think of two peoples sharing one promise find Paul speaking of a joined family, not a replaced one. The verse itself does not use the word "Israel" of the Gentiles.

a: I will call 'my people' those who are not my people
t: Hosea: rejection and return of the northern kingdom
p: Hosea's words were about disowned Israel; Paul applies them to Gentiles.
b: Hosea gave his children the names "Not-loved" and "Not-my-people" to announce that God was breaking with the northern kingdom in the 700s BC, and then promised to reverse the names (Hosea 1:9-10; Hosea 2:23). Paul quotes the promise (mainly Hosea 2:23 and 1:10, in a Greek form that differs a little from the Septuagint) and applies it to Gentiles whom God now calls "my people." Is that a misuse? Views: (1) Paul reads a pattern: the God who restored disowned Israel will also receive the nations (Moo, Dunn); (2) Paul applies Hosea to Jews and Gentiles alike, since both were called (9:24). 1 Peter 2:10 uses the same line of Gentile Christians.

a: only the remnant will be saved
t: Isaiah 10:22-23: the remnant that returns
p: Isaiah's son was named "A remnant will return." Paul uses the idea to say that Israel's story has always been about a surviving core.
b: Paul blends Hosea 1:10 ("The Israelites will be so many that no one can measure or count them, like the sand of the sea") with Isaiah 10:22. This site's Plain of the Hebrew reads: "Even if your people, Israel, were like the sand of the sea, it is a remnant of them that will return" (Isaiah 10:22). The Hebrew has "return" (yashuv), echoing the name of Isaiah's son Shear-jashub (Isaiah 7:3). The Septuagint has "will be saved." Paul follows the Greek, so "return" turns into "be saved." In Isaiah, the "remnant" means those who survive the Assyrian invasion; in Paul it grows into those who respond to the gospel. See also the topic page on the remnant.

a: carry out his word on the earth
t: A hard verse, and a longer Byzantine text
p: The Greek of Isaiah 10:23 is difficult. Paul's short form and the longer Byzantine form read differently.
b: Isaiah 10:23 in this site's Plain reads: "For an end, a settled end, is what the Lord GOD of Armies is about to bring about in the middle of the whole land" (Isaiah 10:23). Paul gives a short form. "Completing and cutting short" (synteleo and syntemno) can mean God will act completely and quickly, or that he will complete the sentence by cutting the people to a remnant. The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) add words that come from the Septuagint; the variant entry shows them. English translations differ widely here, because the Greek can be taken as "quickly" or "completely." The Plain keeps both verbs.
orig: συντελῶν καὶ συντέμνων (synteleon kai syntemnon), 'completing and cutting short'

a: Lord of Armies
t: Lord Sabaoth
p: The Greek writes the Hebrew "of Armies" in Greek letters, Sabaoth.
b: The Greek has kyrios sabaoth, the Hebrew tseva'ot ("armies") written in Greek letters. The Septuagint more often translates it "Lord Almighty," but in Isaiah 1:9 it keeps Sabaoth. The title may mean Israel's armies, the angels or the stars. It appears elsewhere in the New Testament only in James 5:4. The title in Isaiah 1:9 comes from the Jerusalem of 701 BC, when the city survived Sennacherib's siege almost alone (Isaiah 1:7-9).

a: we would have become like Sodom
t: Isaiah 1:9: a few survivors
p: Isaiah looked at a ruined countryside and said only a handful had been spared.
b: In Isaiah's day Assyria had left Judah's countryside burned and Jerusalem standing alone like a shelter in a vineyard (Isaiah 1:8). This site's Plain of the Hebrew: "Had the LORD of Armies not left a handful of us alive, we would have become like Sodom, we would look just like Gomorrah" (Isaiah 1:9). The Septuagint has "offspring" (sperma) where the Hebrew has "survivors." Paul picks that word up: "descendants." It sends the reader back to the "seed" of Abraham (9:7-8). A seed that is left alive is the promise's continued life.

a: laid hold of righteousness
t: What does "righteousness" mean from 9:30 on?
p: Paul uses "righteousness" in at least three senses in the next ten verses. Telling them apart helps.
b: In 9:30-10:6 "righteousness" is (a) a status before God, "being counted in the right," the Reformation sense; (b) a way of living, faithful obedience, as in 10:5; and (c) God's own righteousness (10:3), which can mean the status he gives, his own just character or his faithfulness to his covenant. Wright and Dunn stress that for Paul "righteousness" is about covenant membership: Gentiles have been declared part of God's people without circumcision. The Reformation reading stresses acquittal before a holy judge. Both agree that Gentiles did not chase it and received it, while Israel chased it and missed. The word "faith" explains the difference.

a: a law of righteousness
t: "A law of righteousness": what is it?
p: The phrase can mean a law that promises righteousness, or a law that is itself the standard of being right with God.
b: The Greek says "law of righteousness" and then "did not arrive at law," leaving out "of righteousness" the second time (the Byzantine text supplies it; see the variant entry). Readings: (1) the law as the Torah, which promised life to those who kept it (Moo, Cranfield: Israel pursued righteousness by works and missed); (2) the law pursued as an identity marker, so that Israel missed the law's own goal, which points to Christ (Dunn, Wright); (3) "law" in the sense of principle: Israel pursued righteousness by the principle of law and never reached it. In every reading the failure is that Israel "pursued" (9:31) but not "by faith" (9:32). Moo adds that the meaning of "law" here connects to 10:4.
orig: νόμον δικαιοσύνης (nomon dikaiosynes), 'a law of righteousness'

a: as if it came by works
t: "By works" and "works of the law"
p: "As if by works" is Paul's phrase for a mistaken way of pursuing righteousness.
b: The word "as if" (hos) means "on the supposition that it could come by works." The Byzantine text adds "of the law." For Paul's "works of the law" see 3:20, 28, where the main readings are listed: the deeds the law requires (Moo, Cranfield, Luther) and the boundary markers of Jewish identity such as circumcision, Sabbath and food laws (Dunn, Wright). Here the point is clear without deciding: the issue is not whether Israel obeyed, but that it sought righteousness in a way that did not rest on the promise and its fulfillment in Christ.

a: a stone that makes people stumble and a rock that makes them fall
t: Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16: two stones joined
p: Paul welds two Isaiah verses into one. In Isaiah, the stone is both a refuge and a trap.
b: Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a laid stone, a foundation, and promises that whoever believes will not hurry or panic. This site's Plain: "Look, I have laid a stone in Zion for a foundation, a stone that has been tested, a cornerstone of great worth, a foundation firmly laid. Whoever believes will not hurry" (Isaiah 28:16). Isaiah 8:14 says the LORD "will become a holy place, and a stone that people strike their foot on, and a rock they trip over, for both houses of Israel" (Isaiah 8:14). The Septuagint of 28:16 reads "will not be put to shame," which Paul follows. The same two texts are combined in 1 Peter 2:6-8, and Jesus quoted the "stone the builders rejected" of Psalm 118:22 (Matthew 21:42). Who is the stone? Paul means Christ, as 10:11 shows. In Isaiah 8:14 the stone is the LORD himself. Paul's Christology and his reading of Isaiah are joined here.

a: zeal for God
t: Zeal: Phinehas, Elijah, the Maccabees and Paul himself
p: "Zeal" was a Jewish word for fierce loyalty to God's law, and Paul had been zealous too.
b: The Old Testament holds up zealots: Phinehas, who stopped a plague by killing a man and a woman who defied the covenant, was "zealous for his God" (Numbers 25:13); Elijah said, "I have burned with zeal for the LORD, the God of Armies" (1 Kings 19:10). In the time of the Maccabees zeal meant armed defense of the law (1 Maccabees 2:26-27, 50). Paul describes his own past the same way: "I was zealous for God, the same as every one of you is today" (Acts 22:3; compare Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:6). So when he says Israel has "zeal for God" he is not condescending. He is describing himself before Damascus. The fault he names is not lack of passion but missing "knowledge" (epignosis), the full recognition of what God was doing in Christ.
r: Numbers 25:13; 1 Kings 19:10; 1 Maccabees 2:26; Acts 22:3; Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:6

a: They did not know God's righteousness
t: "God's righteousness": four readings
p: The phrase appears at the start (1:17) and the heart (3:21-26) of the letter. Here it is the thing Israel did not submit to.
b: Dikaiosyne theou can mean (1) the status of righteousness that God gives to those who believe (Luther, much Protestant tradition: a "gift"); (2) God's own justice, the quality that makes him judge fairly; (3) God's faithfulness to his covenant promises, his saving righteousness (Wright, building on the Old Testament use in Psalms and Isaiah 40-55); (4) God's saving power in action (Käsemann). For the long discussion see Romans 1:17 and 3:21-26. In 10:3 the phrase is set against "their own righteousness," which favors reading (1): a righteousness that comes from God against one that comes from the self. Readings (2) and (3) fit "submit to," as one submits to a ruler's plan. The Plain keeps the plain words "God's righteousness" so that all four can be heard.

a: a righteousness of their own
t: "Their own": private achievement or national possession?
p: Paul says Israel was trying to set up a righteousness of its own. The old reading and the New Perspective differ on what "own" means.
b: Two readings. (1) Self-made: "their own" means earned by their own efforts, the Reformation view (Luther, Calvin; Moo). Paul says something similar of himself in Philippians 3:9: "not having a righteousness of my own, the kind that comes from the law." (2) Held as a national privilege: "their own" means belonging to Israel alone, a status they thought was reserved for Jews and not open to Gentiles (Dunn, Wright, and in a different way Stendahl, who argued that Paul's problem was never a guilty conscience). On either reading the contrast is with "God's" righteousness, offered to all who believe (10:4, 11-12).

a: the end of the law
t: "The end of the law": termination, goal or fulfillment?
p: The Greek word telos means end in two senses at once: where something stops, and what it is aiming at.
b: Telos can be (1) the end point, termination (Luther; Sanders; Moo in the sense that the law as a covenant has ended); (2) the goal or aim, as in an archer's target (Cranfield, Badenas; the Latin finis in the Vulgate, which also meant both); (3) the fulfillment or completion, the climax of the story (Wright, The Climax of the Covenant; Jesus says he has come to "fulfill" the law in Matthew 5:17). Many readers hold two or all three together, because the word allows it. "Paul within Judaism" readings (Gager, Nanos): Paul writes to Gentiles, so Christ ends the law as a requirement for the nations, while it stays Israel's own way of life. The key word in the verse is "for everyone who believes": the end of the law brings righteousness to all, not only to those born under it. The Gentile-mission reading says that Christ ends the law's role of dividing Jew from Gentile (Ephesians 2:14-16).
r: Matthew 5:17; Romans 3:31; Romans 6:14; Romans 7:4-6; Galatians 3:24-25; Ephesians 2:14-16

a: Moses writes that the person who does the righteousness
t: Leviticus 18:5: "he will live by them"
p: Paul puts Leviticus on one side and Deuteronomy on the other. Whether they really conflict is disputed.
b: The quotation is Leviticus 18:5. This site's Plain reads: "Keep my rules and my rulings. If a human being does them, he will live by them. I am the LORD" (Leviticus 18:5). Elsewhere it is echoed in Ezekiel 20 and Nehemiah 9:29, and Paul uses it in Galatians 3:12. In the Jewish tradition, "live by them" was taken to mean a life of keeping the commandments, not of dying for them (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 85b and Sanhedrin 74a). Readings: (1) The law's way of righteousness demands perfect obedience and no one has it (traditional Reformation reading); (2) "the righteousness from the law" is a rival route Israel took, a way rooted in the nation's identity (Wright); (3) Paul does not oppose the two quotations but reads both as the same Torah speaking, once in Leviticus and once in Deuteronomy (Hays and others). In (3), 10:6-8 are the Torah's own answer to 10:5. The Greek text varies at this verse; see the variant entry. The Plain follows the SBLGNT.
r: Leviticus 18:5; Ezekiel 20:11; Nehemiah 9:29; Galatians 3:12; Romans 2:13; Romans 7:10

a: Do not say in your heart
t: Deuteronomy 30:12-14: how Paul reads Moses
p: Paul takes a passage about the nearness of God's command and says it describes Christ and the message about him.
b: The source is Deuteronomy 30:12-14, spoken to Israel on the plains of Moab. This site's Plain: "It is not in the sky, so that you would ask, 'Who will climb up into the sky for us and get it, and tell it to us so we can do it?'" (Deuteronomy 30:12). Paul changes "beyond the sea" to "the abyss" and adds "that is, to bring Christ down." Readings: (1) a pesher-style application of the text to Christ, as the Qumran commentaries applied texts to their own time; (2) Christ is now identified with the Torah, as Wisdom had been (Baruch 3:29-30 asks who has gone up to heaven and taken her); (3) Deuteronomy 30 promises return from exile and a circumcised heart (Deuteronomy 30:1-6), which Paul sees fulfilled in the gospel (Wright, Hays). Jewish reading: "It is not in heaven," so a human court decides what the law means (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b); the Palestinian Targums picture Moses and Jonah making the two journeys.

a: the abyss
t: The deep
p: "Abyss" is the Greek word for the deep waters below the earth, the place of the dead.
b: Abyssos means "bottomless": the ocean depths or the realm of the dead below. In the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew tehom, the deep of Genesis 1:2. Luke uses it for the prison of demons (Luke 8:31) and Revelation for the pit (Revelation 9:1; 20:1-3). Paul's gloss, "to bring Christ up from the dead," ties this to the resurrection.

a: the word of faith which we proclaim
t: "The word of faith"
p: "Word" here is rhema, the spoken message. It means both what is said and the believing that answers it.
b: Paul says the nearness of the word ("in your mouth and in your heart") is the gospel message that he preaches. "Of faith" can mean the message that asks for faith or the message about faith. The two organs, mouth and heart, match the two actions of 10:9. The word rhema returns in 10:17 ("the word of Christ"), so the whole passage is built around speaking and hearing.
orig: ῥῆμα τῆς πίστεως (rhema tes pisteos), 'word of faith'

a: Jesus as Lord
t: "Jesus is Lord": the first Christian confession
p: The shortest creed of the New Testament set Jesus where Rome placed the emperor and where Israel placed the LORD.
b: "Jesus is Lord" (kyrios Iesous) is probably the earliest Christian confession (1 Corinthians 12:3; Philippians 2:11; Acts 2:36). It had two backgrounds. In the Greek Bible kyrios stands where Hebrew has the divine name YHWH, so to confess Jesus as kyrios was to speak of him in words reserved for the God of Israel. And in the Roman world "Lord" was a title for the emperor; at the arrest of Polycarp in about AD 155 the officials urged him to say "Caesar is Lord" (Martyrdom of Polycarp 8.2). Käsemann and others have asked whether the verse reflects a baptismal liturgy, in which the new believer said the creed aloud; it is a view, not a fact. The accusative "Jesus as Lord" is the best-supported Greek (see the variant entry).

a: raised him from the dead
t: Why the resurrection is named
p: Faith's content is not a general belief in God but the claim that God raised Jesus.
b: The resurrection is the second half of the creed. Paul had already linked it to Abraham's faith in a God "who gives life to the dead" (4:17, 24) and to Jesus' Sonship (1:4). Here it is the content of the heart's belief, as "Jesus is Lord" is the content of the mouth's confession. Resurrection is what makes "Lord" more than a title: the raised Jesus is the one at God's right hand (Romans 8:34; Acts 2:32-36).

a: No one who believes in him will be put to shame
t: Isaiah 28:16 again, with "everyone"
p: Paul repeats the quotation of 9:33 and adds one word: "everyone."
b: The Septuagint of Isaiah 28:16 says "the one who believes in him will not be put to shame," which Paul quoted in 9:33. The Greek here is "everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame" (the Plain says "no one"), and the addition of "everyone" (pas) turns the promise into the hinge of 10:11-13. The Byzantine text had already put "everyone" into 9:33 (see the variant there). The reader sees the same verse used first to explain Israel's stumbling and now to open the door to anyone. "Put to shame" means to be shown to have trusted in the wrong thing.

a: no difference between Jew and Greek
t: "Greek" means Gentile here
p: Paul pairs "Jew and Greek" as a short way to say "the whole human race" in the Jewish world.
b: "Greek" (Hellen) is the word for any non-Jew, so the Plain keeps Paul's word and adds a gloss. The same phrase marks the beginning of the letter (1:16; 2:9-10; 3:9) and its theme in 3:22: "there is no difference." The point here is that the same Lord is "rich" to all. "Rich toward" echoes 2:4 and returns in 11:33 ("the riches"). Jewish readers hear in "the same Lord of all" the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4): the God of Israel is the God of all nations, which is why Paul can speak of the one Lord for both.

a: anyone at all who calls on the Lord's name
t: Joel 2:32: YHWH's name, said of Jesus
p: Joel promised rescue to anyone who calls on the name of the LORD. Paul applies it to Jesus.
b: The quotation is Joel 2:32 (3:5 in the Hebrew numbering). In Hebrew the verse says "whoever calls on the name of YHWH"; the Greek has kyrios for the name. After 10:9, "the Lord" in 10:12-13 is Jesus, so Paul applies a text about YHWH to Jesus. Acts 2:21 quotes the same verse at Pentecost, and this site's Plain of that verse reads: "anyone at all who calls on the Lord's name will be saved" (Acts 2:21). Richard Bauckham argues that this is a central example of how the first Christians placed Jesus within the unique identity of the one God. The Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant mainstream read this as a statement of Christ's divine identity; Unitarian traditions (such as the Racovian Catechism) read it as honor given to Jesus as God's appointed Lord. On either reading the text puts Jesus in the place Joel gave to the LORD.
r: Joel 2:32; Acts 2:21; Acts 2:38; 1 Corinthians 1:2; Philippians 2:10-11; Isaiah 45:23

a: someone they have never heard
t: "Never heard" him, or never heard of him?
p: The Greek can mean they have not heard about him, or that they have not heard him himself speaking.
b: The phrase is hou ouk ekousan, with a genitive after "hear." In Greek, "hear" with the genitive of a person usually means to hear that person speak. So the verse can read, "How can they believe in the one they have not heard?" The idea would be that in the gospel's proclamation the voice of Christ himself is heard (Ephesians 2:17, where Christ "came and announced the good news"). Some commentators take the verse this way; many translations choose "heard of." Both are possible. Note the chain: call, believe, hear, proclaim, send. It goes backwards from salvation to the sending, and the last link is God's sending, not human choice.
orig: οὗ οὐκ ἤκουσαν (hou ouk ekousan), 'of whom they did not hear / whom they did not hear'

a: How lovely are the feet of those who tell the good news of good things
t: Isaiah 52:7: the herald of good news
p: Both the Hebrew and the Septuagint have one herald; Paul makes it plural for the apostles.
b: Isaiah 52:7 in this site's Plain: "How lovely on the mountains are the feet of the one who brings good news, who makes peace heard, who brings news of good things, who makes salvation heard, who tells Zion, 'Your God is King!'" (Isaiah 52:7). A herald runs across the hills to tell Jerusalem that the exile is over and God is king. Paul changes the singular "the one" to the plural "those" (the Hebrew and the Septuagint both have one herald) and applies it to the apostles and missionaries sent with the gospel. A Qumran text, 11QMelchizedek, also read this verse, taking the herald to be an "anointed one of the Spirit" who announces the end of the age. The Greek verb euangelizomai ("tell the good news") is the verb behind "gospel" (euangelion) throughout the New Testament; its source in Isaiah 40-66 is why it is so rich.

a: Lord, who has believed our report?
t: Isaiah 53:1: the Servant song
p: The prophet's own complaint, in the song of the suffering servant, becomes Paul's explanation for Israel's unbelief.
b: Isaiah 53:1 in this site's Plain reads: "Who has believed what we have heard? And the LORD's arm: to whom has it been shown?" (Isaiah 53:1). John 12:38 quotes the same verse to explain the unbelief of Jesus' hearers. Paul uses it for the same purpose. The Greek akoe can mean "hearing" (what is heard) or "report" (what is said), which sets up the word play in 10:17: "faith comes from akoe, and akoe through the word of Christ." Note also that "obey" (hypakouo, from the same root as "hear") is how Paul describes the right response to the gospel, in line with "the obedience of faith" (1:5; 16:26).

a: faith comes from listening
t: "The word of Christ": from him or about him?
p: The little genitive "of Christ" can mean the word Christ speaks or the word about him.
b: Rhematos Christou can be (1) an objective genitive, the message about Christ; (2) a subjective genitive, a message that Christ himself speaks through his messengers (compare the note on 10:14); or (3) "a word that comes by Christ's command." Some manuscripts read "the word of God" (see the variant). The saying became important in Protestant teaching on the preached word as the means of faith: the Second Helvetic Confession (chapter 1) says that the preaching of the word of God is the word of God. Catholic and Orthodox teaching also treat preaching as a way grace is given, together with the sacraments.

a: Their voice has gone out into the whole earth
t: Psalm 19:4: the heavens, or the apostles?
p: The Psalm is about the sky telling God's glory. Paul uses its words for the spread of the gospel.
b: This site's Plain of the Hebrew of Psalm 19:4 reads: "Yet their line has run out over the whole earth, their words to the world's edge" (Psalm 19:4). The Hebrew word is qav ("line," a measuring cord); the Septuagint has phthongos ("sound"), as if it read qol, "voice." Paul follows the Greek. Views: (1) "they" are the preachers of the gospel and the verse is used as an image of its worldwide reach (Moo, Dunn), so that Israel, scattered through the empire, has heard; (2) the voice is creation's witness, as in the Psalm (compare 1:19-20), and Paul says it shows that no one is without a witness to God; (3) it is a rhetorical flourish, with no one-to-one claim. Paul's question is whether Israel "did not hear." His answer is that they did hear; the problem is something else (10:19-21).

a: I myself will stir you to jealousy by those who are no nation
t: Deuteronomy 32:21: the Song of Moses
p: Moses sang that God would answer Israel's jealousy-provoking idols by making Israel jealous of another people.
b: The line comes from the Song of Moses. This site's Plain: "They stirred my jealousy with a not-god and angered me with their puffs of air. So I will stir their jealousy with a not-people, and anger them with a nation of fools" (Deuteronomy 32:21). Israel made God jealous with idols; God will make Israel jealous with a people who are not a people. Paul reads "not-people" as the Gentiles, and "jealous" is the thread of 11:11 and 11:14. The Septuagint has "no nation" (ep' ouk ethnei), which Paul follows. Richard Bell has argued that the whole of Romans 9-11 is shaped by this verse. The Song of Moses is also in the background of 12:19 (Deuteronomy 32:35) and 15:10 (Deuteronomy 32:43).

a: Those who were not looking for me found me
t: Isaiah 65:1: who is "a nation not called by my name"?
p: In its own chapter, the verse may be about Israel. Paul reads the Greek order as speaking of Gentiles.
b: Isaiah 65:1 in this site's Plain: "I let myself be asked by those who did not ask; I let myself be found by those who did not look for me. I said, 'I am here, I am here,' to a nation that was not called by my name" (Isaiah 65:1). In the Hebrew, the "nation" is probably rebellious Israel itself (the next verse speaks of "a rebellious people"); the Hebrew can be read as "I was ready to be sought by a people who did not ask." Paul reads 65:1 as the Gentiles and 65:2 as Israel (10:21). "Goes so far as to say" (apotolmai) means Paul admires Isaiah's courage in saying something so sharp. Paul swaps the two lines of the Septuagint so that the second line is first.

a: I have stretched out my hands
t: Isaiah 65:2: the open hands
p: God reaches out all day, and the people he reaches for talk back.
b: This site's Plain of Isaiah 65:2: "I have spread out my hands all day long toward a rebellious people, who walk the road that is not good" (Isaiah 65:2). Paul keeps the picture of outstretched hands, a gesture of invitation like a parent calling a child. "All day long" matters: God's offer to Israel never lapsed. The two participles "disobey" and "talk back" (apeitheo, antilego) describe the response. The verse prepares for 11:1: even rebellious Israel is still the people to whom God holds out his hands.

a: did God push his people away?
t: Psalm 94:14 and 1 Samuel 12:22: God does not abandon his people
p: Paul's question and its answer borrow the language of two older promises.
b: Two verses lie behind the question and 11:2. This site's Plain of the Psalm: "For the LORD will not let go of his people; he will not walk away from his inheritance" (Psalm 94:14). Samuel had said to a frightened people: "The LORD will not walk away from his people. His great name is at stake" (1 Samuel 12:22). Paul's "push away" (apotheo) is the verb of the Septuagint of Psalm 94:14. In both older texts God's promise holds even though the people have sinned. So the question that opens chapter 11 is not new: it is the question those verses already answered. "By no means!" (see the note at 9:14) is Paul's reply in the diatribe style.

a: I am an Israelite myself, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin
t: Paul as proof: a Jew who believes
p: Paul offers himself as the first piece of evidence. He is a Jewish believer, so God has not dropped the Jews.
b: Benjamin was the tribe of Israel's first king, Saul, whose name Paul shared (1 Samuel 9:1-2; Acts 13:21), and of the loyal tribe that stayed with Judah after Solomon. Paul says the same about himself in Philippians 3:5 and 2 Corinthians 11:22. Krister Stendahl, in Paul among Jews and Gentiles, stressed that Paul never speaks of leaving Judaism and calls his Damascus experience a call, not a conversion; this verse is one of his supports. Others (Segal, Paul the Convert) see a real break. Either way, Paul argues in the logic of the remnant: the proof that God has not rejected Israel is that Israelites are in the church.

a: whom he knew beforehand
t: "Knew beforehand" of a whole people
p: The same verb Paul used in 8:29 is here said of Israel. That matters for the debate about election.
b: Proegno is the verb of 8:29, "those he knew beforehand he also decided beforehand." In Hebrew, "to know" (yada) often means to choose or to care for, as when God says he has "known" only Israel of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). Here the object is not a list of believers but "his people," so the verb looks like election of a nation. Calvinist readers take it as electing love without reference to merit; Arminian and Wesleyan readers take "knew beforehand" as foreknowledge of faith in 8:29, while others ask whether foreknown faith fits 11:2, where the object is the whole people; Catholic and Orthodox readers combine foreknowledge with God's saving will. See the notes at Romans 8:29-30 for the verb itself.

a: seven thousand men
t: 1 Kings 19: the seven thousand and the remnant
p: When Elijah thought he was alone, God said he had kept seven thousand.
b: Elijah, on Horeb after the contest on Carmel, says he is the only faithful one left (1 Kings 19:10, 14). God answers: "But I will keep seven thousand left in Israel: every knee that has not bent to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him" (1 Kings 19:18). Paul changes the future "I will keep" to "I have left for myself," putting the sparing already in the past, and he adds "for myself": the remnant is God's own doing. The number seven thousand is a round, complete number (seven times a thousand). In Paul's time the remnant is Jewish believers, among whom Paul counts himself. Like Elijah, Paul may be tempted to think he is alone; the point is that he is not.

a: a remnant has come to be
t: The remnant in Isaiah, Qumran and Paul
p: A remnant is the small group that carries a larger story forward. Paul counts Jewish believers as that group in his time.
b: The idea runs from Noah's family through Isaiah's son Shear-jashub ("a remnant will return," Isaiah 7:3; 10:20-22) to the survivors of exile (Ezra 9:8). The Qumran community also called itself the remnant that God left (Damascus Document 1:4-5). Paul's "remnant" in the present is those Jews who have believed in Jesus. The remnant is not only a number. It is a pledge that the rest has not been lost for good (11:15-16), because a firstfruit and a root belong to the whole. See also the topic page on the remnant.
r: Isaiah 7:3; Isaiah 10:20-22; 2 Kings 19:30-31; Ezra 9:8; Damascus Document 1:4-5

a: chosen by grace
t: "Election of grace": what does grace rule out?
p: Paul says the remnant exists by grace. He means that no one earned a place in it.
b: Kat' eklogen charitos, "according to a choice of grace," gives grace as the reason for the choice. All traditions agree that the remnant is not earned. They differ on how God's choosing relates to human response. Reformed churches teach that God chooses persons unconditionally and grace overcomes the will (Westminster Confession 3 and 10; Canons of Dort I). Lutherans teach election in Christ without a doctrine of a decree of rejection (Formula of Concord XI). The Council of Trent held that no work or faith before justification earns it (decree on justification, chapter 8). Orthodox and Wesleyan traditions stress that grace is offered to all and can be refused. See the card on election at 9:11.

a: it no longer comes from works
t: Grace and works: the line between them
p: If something is a gift, it cannot also be a wage. Paul uses that rule to describe how the remnant exists.
b: The argument matches 4:4-5, where wages are "owed" and grace is a gift. Here it explains why the remnant is by grace, not by Jewish heritage or obedience. Debate arises about what "works" are: all human deeds (the Reformation reading), or the specific marks of Jewish identity (Dunn, Wright). The Byzantine text adds a second sentence making the same point from the other side (see the variant entry). Tradition differences are for the justification card at Romans 3:21; here the stress falls on why the remnant is a sign of grace.

a: hardened
t: Two words for hardening: sklerynei and poroo
p: In 9:18 Paul wrote "makes hard." Here the verb is a different one, taken from a word for a callus.
b: Poroo comes from poros, a hard stone or a callus on a bone or skin; in medical Greek it can mean the hardening of a joint or of tissue. It is the word of Mark 3:5 ("their hearts had turned so hard," Mark 3:5), Mark 6:52 and John 12:40, and of 2 Corinthians 3:14, where "their minds were hardened." The noun porosis appears in 11:25. The passive "were hardened" (eporothesan) is the divine passive: someone hardened them, and in 11:8 that someone is God. The older Pharaoh word (sklerynei, 9:18) and this word both belong to the topic page on the hardening of the heart. This is not a final verdict: 11:11 insists the stumble is not a fall, and 11:25 says the hardening is for a time.
r: Mark 3:5; Mark 6:52; John 12:40; 2 Corinthians 3:14; Romans 9:18; Romans 11:25

a: a spirit of numbness
t: Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10 woven together
p: Paul joins two Old Testament texts about a people who could not see or hear and says the same has happened in his day.
b: The first is from Moses' speech: "Yet to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to know with, eyes to see with or ears to hear with" (Deuteronomy 29:4). The second is from Isaiah: "For the LORD has poured a spirit of deep sleep over you; he has closed your eyes, the prophets, and covered your heads, the visionaries" (Isaiah 29:10). The Septuagint of Isaiah has katanyxis ("stupor," a state of being pierced, dazed); the Plain chooses "numbness." "Down to this very day" is from Deuteronomy. Notice that Moses speaks this right before the covenant renewal in Moab: even in the best days of Israel there was a blindness that God had not yet removed. Isaiah's sense is similar, and Isaiah 6:9-10 (quoted in Acts 28:26-27) is the best-known passage in this family.

a: David says
t: Psalm 69:22-23: a prayer against enemies, turned on Israel
p: Paul uses a psalm of a suffering righteous man against enemies. He applies it to Israel's unbelief.
b: Psalm 69 is one of the New Testament's favorite psalms of the righteous sufferer (John 2:17; John 15:25; Romans 15:3). Verses 22-23 call down judgment on the psalmist's enemies. This site's Plain reads: "Let their table in front of them become a trap, and for their friends a snare. Let their eyes grow dark so they cannot see, and make their hips shake all the time" (Psalm 69:22-23). Paul changes "hips" to "backs." What is "the table"? Views: the blessings of Israel's life, which became a trap (the covenant privileges of 9:4); the Temple meals; or the table as a place of security. Many read this as a curse on those who persecuted Christ, since Psalm 69 is a psalm about him. A reader troubled by a curse here should read the topic page on the curse psalms and 11:11, where the "stumble" is explained as not final.

a: did they stumble so that they would fall?
t: Stumbling is not falling
p: Paul separates two words: stumble and fall. The first can be recovered from, the second cannot.
b: The Greek has eptaisan ("stumbled") and pesosin ("fall"). The question is whether Israel's stumble was meant to end in a final fall. "So that" (hina) can express purpose or result. Most take it as result: did they stumble with the result that they fell for good? Paul's word for the stumble in 11:11-12 is the noun paraptoma, "trespass," the same word as in 5:15-20. The answer "By no means!" shows that Paul sees Israel's unbelief as a stumble with a purpose beyond itself: salvation for the Gentiles, and then, through the Gentiles' jealousy, a return. This is the argument from 11:11 to 11:15. Readers who take Paul's "By no means!" at face value find the later teaching that Israel has fallen for good hard to square with it. See the deep dive on this chapter.

a: their fullness
t: Israel's "fullness" and "defeat"
p: Two rare words: hettema (defeat or loss) and pleroma (fullness). Both are disputed.
b: Hettema appears in Isaiah 31:8 in the Septuagint (a defeat of Assyria) and in 1 Corinthians 6:7 (a "defeat," a failure). It can mean a diminishing or a defeat, so some read "loss." Pleroma means "fullness" or "full number." For Israel it can be (a) their full number, the return of the many who now are out (the usual reading, Moo, Cranfield); (b) their full obedience or full inclusion; (c) their full place in God's plan. Paul sets it against 11:25, the "full number" of the Gentiles. The argument is "how much more": if a stumble helped the world, a recovery will help the world more.

a: I am an apostle of the Gentiles
t: Paul speaks to the Gentiles in Rome
p: Paul pauses to address the Gentile Christians directly and tells them why he cares for Israel.
b: Until 11:13 Paul has argued in general. Now he turns to "you Gentiles," the likely majority in the Roman churches after the Jews were expelled under Claudius (on the expulsion under Claudius see Acts 18:2). He tells them that his Gentile mission and his love of his people are one thing: by honoring his mission to the Gentiles he hopes to move his own people (11:14). The title "apostle of the Gentiles" matches Galatians 2:7-9, where Peter was entrusted with the mission to the circumcised and Paul with the mission to the uncircumcised, and Acts 9:15 and 22:21.

a: my own flesh and blood
t: "My flesh": Paul's own family
p: "Flesh" in Hebrew speech can mean family or kin.
b: The Greek says "my flesh." In the Old Testament "my flesh" is a way to say "my kin" (Genesis 29:14; 2 Samuel 5:1 "your bone and your flesh"). The Plain keeps the picture. Paul does not claim to save anyone: "save" here means that God will use his work. Note the modest "some." He expects only some in his lifetime. The larger hope comes at 11:26.
orig: μου τὴν σάρκα (mou ten sarka), 'my flesh'

a: life from the dead
t: "Life from the dead": resurrection or renewal?
p: The phrase can mean the final resurrection or a great renewal of the world.
b: Two main readings. (1) The final resurrection: Israel's acceptance will mark the end of the age, when the dead are raised (Cranfield, Moo; "from the dead" is Paul's usual language for resurrection, as in 1 Corinthians 15:12, though the phrase "life from the dead" is found only here). (2) A figure for great spiritual renewal: Israel's turning will bring new life to the world as if from death (Calvin takes it so in his commentary on this verse). Paul does not say. The Greek has no definite article. The parallel "reconciliation of the world" in the first half of the verse is a present event, which may favor a present or near renewal, though the phrase "from the dead" is the standard phrase for resurrection.

a: If the firstfruit is holy
t: The dough offering and the root
p: Paul uses two pictures of a part that stands for the whole: dough and a tree.
b: The first picture is the first loaf from a batch of dough, set aside for the LORD: "From the first of your dough, set aside a loaf as a gift" (Numbers 15:20). The gift makes the whole batch holy. The second picture is the root of a tree. Who is the firstfruit and the root? Views: (1) the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (11:28), the most common; (2) the Jewish believers who are the first harvest (the remnant of 11:5); (3) Abraham alone; (4) Christ. The two pictures may point to different things, the first to the first believers and the second to the patriarchs. In any case, the argument runs from the part to the whole: the rest of Israel is holy because of the root.

a: a wild olive
t: Olive trees, grafting and Paul's picture
p: Olive grafting was a known skill. Paul's picture runs the usual order backward on purpose.
b: The olive tree is a biblical image of Israel: in Jeremiah 11:16 God calls his people a green olive tree with fair fruit. In Paul's picture, the cultivated tree is Israel; its broken-off branches are Jews who did not believe; the wild olive branch is the Gentile believer, grafted among the others. Ancient farm writers describe grafting a wild olive shoot onto a tired cultivated tree to renew it (Columella, On Agriculture 5.9.16, as discussed by Baxter and Ziesler), so the picture is not nonsense. But the normal order is to graft a cultivated branch onto a wild stock. Paul says this himself in 11:24 ("against nature"). The point of the strangeness is that God's way with Gentiles is unexpected.

a: you are not holding up the root. The root is holding you up
t: The warning to the Gentiles: one tree, not two
p: Paul tells Gentile believers that they depend on Israel's root, not the other way round.
b: The image has only one tree. Gentiles are grafted into it; they do not form a new tree beside it, and the tree was not cut down. Readings of the picture: (1) Israel and the church are one people of God with Gentiles added, the reading found in much Catholic and Reformed teaching and in Messianic Jewish writing (Kinzer); (2) the church takes the place of the branches that were cut off, the replacement view. Its strongest form does not begin in contempt for Jews. It argues from Galatians 6:16, Philippians 3:3, Ephesians 2:11-22 and 1 Peter 2:9-10 that the titles of Israel now belong to those who are in Christ, and from Hebrews 8 that the old covenant has given way to the new; the fathers (Justin) called the church the true Israel. Its critics reply that Paul's warning here is aimed at exactly that boast, and that he never says the branches are gone for good (11:23); (3) a Jewish-Gentile partnership, in which the Gentiles receive Israel's blessings while Israel keeps its own calling (Stendahl, Gager, Nanos). The history of how Gentile Christians boasted over Jews anyway is the reason the church leaders of the 20th century returned to this verse (Nostra Aetate 4 cites it). See the deep dive on supersessionism.

a: it is by faith that you stand
t: "Do not think highly of yourself. Be afraid instead"
p: Paul tells Gentile believers to be humble because they stand by faith, which is not their own doing either.
b: The Greek is literally "do not think high things." The same verb of attitude is used in 12:3 and 12:16. "Be afraid" is the fear of the LORD, not terror, the reverence the Old Testament demands (Proverbs 3:7: "Do not be wise in your own eyes. Fear the LORD, and stay clear of evil"). The same lesson appears in 11:25: "so that you will not think you are wise on your own." The answer to arrogance is not guilt but a clear view of how one came to stand.

a: if you stay in that kindness
t: The warning: can a believer be cut off?
p: Paul warns that Gentile believers too can be cut off. The churches read this very differently.
b: Is the "you" individual believers or the Gentile church as a group? Readings: (1) A real warning that individuals can fall away from salvation (Catholic, Orthodox, Wesleyan and many Lutheran readers; Hebrews 6:4-6 is the parallel); (2) A warning that works as a means: God uses it to keep the elect, who will not in fact fall away (Reformed and many Baptists; Westminster Confession 17); (3) A corporate warning to the Gentile churches as a body, who could lose their place in the way Israel's branches did, without settling the fate of each person (Dunn, Wright, Moo allows this). The traditions card sets these out. Paul does not say how the "if" is fulfilled except by "staying" in God's kindness, which is another way of saying "by faith" (11:20).
orig: ἐπιμένῃς τῇ χρηστότητι (epimenes te chrestoteti), 'continue in the kindness'

a: severity
t: Kindness and severity
p: The Greek for "severity" is a cutting word. It matches the cutting of branches.
b: Apotomia comes from apotemno, "to cut off," so the word means a sharp, cutting-off severity. It appears only here in the New Testament. Paired with chrestotes (kindness, the word of 2:4), it describes God in two directions at once. Paul's point is that both belong to God: those who think of God only as kind miss 11:22a; those who think of him only as severe miss 11:22b. The Vulgate has bonitas and severitas, the source of the English "severity."

a: against nature
t: "Against nature": the same phrase as in chapter 1, a different use
p: Paul uses "against nature" for the grafting, as he did for sexual acts in 1:26. In 11:24 it is God's act that is unnatural.
b: Para physin is "contrary to nature." In 1:26 it describes what Paul counts as a violation; here it describes a wonderful act of God, grafting a wild branch into a cultivated tree. The phrase is therefore not a fixed term of blame in Paul's Greek; it is a description of what goes against the usual order, to be judged by context. For the idea of what is "natural" in the Stoic and Jewish world see Romans 1:26. Paul's "natural branches" and "their own tree" return in the same verse and carry his point: for Israel, being grafted back is an easier thing than the Gentiles' grafting.

a: mystery
t: "Mystery" is a secret now revealed
p: In Paul, a mystery is not a puzzle. It is something hidden in God's plan until he made it known.
b: Mysterion is used in Daniel 2 (Septuagint) of what God reveals to a seer. In Paul it is a plan hidden in God and now made known: the gospel (16:25-26), the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:51), the joining of Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 3:3-6). Here the mystery has two parts: a partial hardening of Israel and its limit in time, and the salvation of all Israel. The grammar "I do not want you to be ignorant" (compare 1:13) is how Paul introduces something important. The point of making it known to the Gentiles is given in the same verse: so that they will not be wise in their own eyes (compare Proverbs 3:7: "Do not be wise in your own eyes").

a: a hardening has come upon part of Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles comes in
t: "In part," "until" and "the full number of the Gentiles"
p: Three small phrases that shape the whole question of Israel's future.
b: (1) "upon part of Israel" (apo merous) can modify the noun (a partial hardening, in extent) or mean "for a while" (in time). Most take it as extent: not all Israel is hardened, as Paul himself shows. (2) "until" (achri hou) fixes a limit: the hardening ends when something happens. Compare Jesus' words, "Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (Luke 21:24). (3) "the full number of the Gentiles" (to pleroma ton ethnon) may mean the full count of Gentiles who will be saved, or the completion of the Gentile mission (Paul's work to Spain, 15:24), or the full inclusion of Gentiles in God's people. "Comes in" (eiserchomai) is a word of entering a house or the kingdom. The question is whether the "until" gives a sequence (first the Gentiles, then Israel) or only a boundary.

a: and so
t: "And so" (houtos): "in this way" or "then"?
p: One small Greek word decides whether Paul gives a way or a time. English "so" can carry either.
b: Houtos normally means "in this way, thus." English Bibles have "and so," but many preachers have heard in it "and then all Israel will be saved" (a sequence: after the Gentiles come in, all Israel). Most modern scholars hold that the word means "in this manner": Israel will be saved in this way, namely by the stumbling that brought in the Gentiles and the jealousy that brings Israel back (Cranfield, Moo, Fitzmyer, Dunn, Wright). They argue that if Paul meant "then" he would have used tote or epeita. Others hold that the word carries both: Israel is saved in this way, and the way ends with a turning after the Gentiles have come in. Because "so" in English holds both, the Plain keeps it. The note on "all Israel" gives the views.

a: all Israel will be saved
t: "All Israel will be saved": who, and how?
p: The most debated sentence in Romans 9-11. Six readings, with their main advocates.
b: (1) The nation of Israel at the end: a large-scale turning of the Jewish people, most of them (not every individual, as in "all Israel" in the Old Testament and rabbinic usage, where "all Israel" means the people as a whole; compare Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1: "All Israel has a share in the world to come"). Held by many commentators since the Reformation and by the Puritans, and by Hodge, Murray, Cranfield, Moo, Dunn and Fitzmyer. (2) The elect of Israel through all history, the remnant gathered in every age (held by some Reformed writers). (3) The whole people of God, Jews and Gentiles together, "Israel" being redefined as in 9:6 (Calvin; N. T. Wright; compare Galatians 6:16). (4) A national restoration of Israel to its land and Messiah (dispensational readings; Scofield). (5) Israel saved by God's covenant in a path of its own, in which Jews are saved by God's faithfulness without a change of religion (the Sonderweg, "special path," Franz Rosenzweig's "two covenants" idea, taken up in various forms by some modern scholars such as Gager and Stendahl; Hvalvik's article criticizes it). (6) Jews who convert through the church's mission, gradually (traditional mission readings). The card on this chapter gives the churches' positions.

a: The Deliverer will come out of Zion
t: Isaiah 59:20-21 and Isaiah 27:9: the Deliverer
p: Paul joins Isaiah 59:20-21 and Isaiah 27:9. Even the first line changes the Hebrew.
b: In this site's Plain the Hebrew of Isaiah 59:20 reads: "A redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from rebellion," the LORD declares (Isaiah 59:20). The Septuagint has "will come for the sake of Zion"; Paul has "out of Zion". A possible reason: Psalm 14:7 and Psalm 53:6 long for salvation for Israel to come out of Zion, and "out of Zion" is the usual way to say God acts from Jerusalem. "Turn from rebellion" becomes "turn ungodliness away from Jacob" (Isaiah 27:9 adds: "So this is how Jacob's guilt will be atoned for, and taking his sin away will bear this fruit," Isaiah 27:9). Who is the Deliverer? Most read Christ and his coming (first or second); some read God himself (the original sense) with Christ as his agent. If "out of Zion" means the second coming from the heavenly Jerusalem, it supports a future turning; if it means the first coming from Zion, it points to the cross.

a: the covenant from me for them
t: Whose covenant? Isaiah 59:21 and Jeremiah 31
p: The "covenant" of this line comes from Isaiah, but its words about sins taken away also echo the new covenant.
b: The line begins like Isaiah 59:21: "As for me, this is my covenant with them," says the LORD (Isaiah 59:21). The second half, "when I take away their sins," echoes Isaiah 27:9 and Jeremiah 31:34: "I will forgive their guilt, and their sin I will remember no more" (Jeremiah 31:34). So the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31-34 is in view. Is that covenant the Abrahamic promise renewed, or the covenant in Christ's blood (1 Corinthians 11:25)? Readings differ: for many Christians, Paul means the new covenant in Jesus, so Israel's salvation comes through him; for readers like Kinzer and Nanos, the covenant is Israel's own covenant with God, and the question is how the nations are joined to it. The text does not say.

a: they are enemies
t: "Enemies": hostile to God, or treated as enemies by God?
p: The Greek word can be active (they oppose) or passive (they are regarded as God's enemies).
b: Echthroi is active in 5:10 ("while we were enemies"). Commentators divide. The pairing with "beloved" (agapetoi) in the same verse, which is passive, leads some to read "enemies" as passive too: treated as enemies by God, for the sake of the Gentiles. Others keep the active sense, as in 5:10: as far as the gospel goes, Israel resists it, for the Gentiles' sake. Paul does not make these two separate statuses; they are two descriptions of one people. A warning: Christian history has often kept "enemies" and forgotten "beloved." Chrysostom's sermons against Judaizers and Luther's 1543 pamphlet On the Jews and Their Lies are examples. The Plain keeps Paul's two words together.

a: From the point of view of election, they are beloved
t: Election and Israel: which "election"?
p: Here "election" refers to the whole people, not to individuals, which affects how the word is read in chapter 9.
b: In 11:5-7 "election" is the chosen remnant inside Israel; in 11:28 it is Israel as a people, loved "for the sake of the patriarchs." The word has a double use within a few verses. Karl Barth made use of this in his teaching on election in Church Dogmatics II/2: God's election is first of all in Christ and of one people, with Israel and the church as its two forms. Reformed tradition more often reads chapters 9 and 11 together as personal election. Dispensationalists read it as proof that Israel as a nation keeps a special calling. A common point across the views is that election is love shown before merit, which 9:11 and 11:28 both say.

a: God does not take back his gifts and his call
t: "Irrevocable": the verse that changed the church's teaching
p: This verse is the main support for the claim that God has not ended his covenant with the Jews, and it is cited in Nostra Aetate 4.
b: The Greek ametameleta means "not to be regretted" or "not to be taken back." It is a legal word. Verses like this one stand behind the Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate 4, which says that the Jews remain most dear to God for the sake of their fathers, because God does not repent of his gifts and calls (Romans 11:28-29). In 1980 at Mainz Pope John Paul II spoke of the Old Covenant as never revoked by God. A document of 2015 by the Vatican's Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews took its title from this verse: The Gifts and the Calling of God Are Irrevocable. The commission says that the text is not a magisterial or doctrinal document. The 1994 declaration of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America to the Jewish community rejected Luther's later attacks on Jews and opposed anti-Semitism; it does not itself speak of covenant. Jewish statements such as Dabru Emet (2000) welcomed the movement. Historically the opposite reading has been common: that the gifts passed to the church. A fair note: the dialogue statements do not agree about what the verse means for the Christian mission to Jews, and many evangelical, Orthodox and Messianic Jewish voices read it differently.

a: you have been shown mercy because they disobeyed
t: The thread of "mercy"
p: The word mercy ties the end of chapter 11 to the start of chapter 9.
b: "Show mercy" (eleeo) is the verb of 9:15, 16 and 18 (9:23 has the noun), now used in 11:30-32 three times. The chapters begin with God's freedom to show mercy to whom he wishes and end with God's mercy toward all. This framing (an inclusio) suggests that the mercy of 9:15-18 is not a threat but the very thing that rescues. In 11:30 the Gentiles are said to have received mercy "because" of Israel's disobedience, and in 11:31 Israel will receive mercy through the mercy shown to the Gentiles. Each group is the occasion of the other's mercy.

a: by the mercy shown to you
t: "By your mercy" goes with which verb?
p: The phrase "to your mercy" can attach either to "disobeyed" or to "may be shown mercy."
b: The Greek is to hymetero eleei, a dative ("to," "by" or "for" your mercy) that can attach to either verb. (1) With "may be shown mercy": "they have disobeyed, so that by the mercy shown to you they also may be shown mercy." This is the common reading, and the Plain follows it: the mercy the Gentiles received becomes the way Israel is reached. (2) With "were disobedient": "they have disobeyed with your mercy in view," so that their disobedience serves the Gentiles' mercy, as 11:30 says.
