The first makes Gentile mercy the means to Israel's mercy; the second makes Israel's disobedience the means to Gentile mercy. The word "now" before the second "mercy" is a variant (see the entry).
orig: τῷ ὑμετέρῳ ἐλέει (to hymetero eleei), 'by/for your mercy'

a: so that he can show mercy to everyone
t: "Mercy to everyone": how wide?
p: Paul ends the argument with a sentence that sounds universal. Christians read it in different ways.
b: "All" is not defined here. Readings: (1) all people without exception will finally be shown mercy: Origen's hope for the restoration of all things, some readings of Gregory of Nyssa, and in the twentieth century Karl Barth and Hans Urs von Balthasar, though Barth denied he taught universal salvation; (2) all kinds of people, Jews and Gentiles as groups (Augustine, Calvin, Reformed readers); (3) the offer is for all and can be refused (Wesley, Arminius, Orthodox and Catholic teaching, which rejects universalism as a doctrine though some theologians hope for it). Both uses are "the all" (tous pantas), which many take to mean both groups, all of them. The sentence closes the section on mercy for these two groups.

a: shut everyone up together
t: "Shut up" like a net or a prison
p: The Greek verb is used of fish in a net and of prisoners.
b: Synkleio means "close in together." It is used of a catch of fish in a net (Luke 5:6) and of the locking-up of a city (Joshua 6:1 in the Septuagint). Galatians 3:22-23 uses it of Scripture shutting up everything under sin. The sense here: God gives both groups the same verdict, disobedient, to bring both to the same mercy.

a: Oh, how deep are God's riches
t: The doxology: where the argument stops
p: Paul ends three chapters of argument with a hymn, because he cannot finish it any other way.
b: Paul has argued, and now he breaks into praise. The three nouns, riches, wisdom, knowledge, and the two adjectives, "unsearchable" and "untraceable" (literally, one cannot follow the footprints), stress limits. The "depth" of God's judgments has an echo in Psalm 36:6: "your judgments, the great deep." The mood is not defeat but wonder. Praise at the limit of understanding has Old Testament models (Job 11:7-9; Psalm 139:6), and Paul closes other sections with a hymn (compare the praise at Romans 16:25-27 and Philippians 4:20). The Greek can be read "the depth of God's riches, and of his wisdom and knowledge" (three things), as the Plain has it, or "the depth of the riches of God's wisdom and knowledge" (the riches are the wisdom and knowledge).
r: Psalm 36:6; Psalm 139:6; Job 11:7-9; Romans 11:34-36; Wisdom of Solomon 9:13

a: For who has come to know the Lord's mind?
t: Isaiah 40:13: nobody advised the LORD
p: Isaiah asked who advised the LORD when he made the world. Paul uses the question for God's plan.
b: This site's Plain of the Hebrew: "Who has taken the measure of the LORD's Spirit? What adviser of his has taught him anything?" (Isaiah 40:13). The Septuagint has "mind" (nous) where the Hebrew has "spirit" (ruach), and Paul follows it. Paul also quotes the same verse in 1 Corinthians 2:16, there adding "but we have the mind of Christ." Wisdom of Solomon 9:13 asks, "What human being can know God's plan?"

a: Or who has given to him first
t: Job 41:11: nobody puts God in debt
p: The question comes from the end of God's speeches in Job. No one can claim a payment from God.
b: Paul's wording does not match the Septuagint of Job 41:3 closely, and does not match the Hebrew exactly. This site's Plain of the Hebrew verse: "Who has ever faced me and then made me repay him? All that is beneath the whole sky belongs to me" (Job 41:11). Most commentators think Job is the source, though the match is loose. The answer is the same: nobody can say God owes them. That ties back to 9:20 and 11:6: grace means no one holds a claim.

a: from him, and through him, and for him
t: A formula Greeks used, and Paul's use of it
p: Greek writers had a similar three-part line about the source of everything. Paul uses it for the God of Israel.
b: The three prepositions ("from, through, to") match a Stoic way of speaking about nature or the world. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, writing later (about AD 170s), addresses nature with a similar line, "from you are all things, in you are all things, to you are all things" (Meditations 4.23). The scholar Eduard Norden collected such formulas in Agnostos Theos (1913). The honest verdict on any link: Paul and the Stoics share a style of speech, but Paul's God is a personal Lord who has acted in history, not the world-soul; Paul may also have taken the pattern from Jewish liturgy. Augustine and other fathers read the three words as pointing to Father, Son and Spirit (On the Trinity); the passage itself says "him," not three persons. 1 Corinthians 8:6 and Colossians 1:16 use similar words of Christ.
